Comment rendre le Mois de l’histoire des: How can Black History Month be made more inclusive?
« Le Mois de l’histoire des Noirs, c’est: “Black History Month is a month of remembrance”
L'image illustre un groupe d'immigrants: The image shows an intergenerational group of immigrants from Quebec’s culturally diverse Black communities. Illustration: Nia E-K
Le Mois de l’histoire des Noirs est deve: Black History Month has received more and more media attention in recent years. Every year, cultural and educational activities are organized during the month to recognize and celebrate the contribution of the Black community in Quebec and Canada. What does this month mean for those who are far from the spotlight, who live in the neighbourhoods? As part of La Converse’s Dialogues, we discussed it with about ten people from Montréal’s Black communities.
C’est un soir de février, dans le fond d: It’s a February evening, at the back of Boutique Espace Urbain, when the dialogue gets underway. Several people from different generations have come to share and exchange their experiences and feelings about Black History Month in this country. As everyone settles in, we notice that two groups are sharing the space: young people from immigrant backgrounds on one side, and older people who recently arrived in Canada on the other.
Questionnés sur leur rapport au Mois de: Asked about their relationship to Black History Month (BHM), the participants in the discussion say they feel a certain unease. A few, however, say that BHM is symbolic for them. That’s the case for Jean Alex, a health-care worker. In his forties and of Haitian origin, he has been living in Quebec for nearly five years. He explains that, “for [him], Black History Month is a month of remembrance for the Black community in Quebec and Canada.” Along the same lines, Sherlyne, a civil servant who once ran in a provincial election, says: “For me, it represents the hidden history of Black people in this country.”
Cette vision des choses de Jean Alex et: Jean Alex and Sherlyne’s view isn’t shared by the rest of the guests. “I hope you’ll excuse my bluntness, but I find all of this hypocritical. Promoting something for a certain period [just one month] and then doing nothing afterwards is very hypocritical,” exclaims Gana, who is finishing her first year as a resident of Quebec.
Pour Gabriela, fondatrice de la librairi: For Gabriela, founder of the bookstore Racines, Black History Month is driven by a capitalist vision. “Everyone cashes in on this month. Instead of looking at the negative, I think we need to take advantage of it to try to shake up the companies and institutions that use Black History Month for capitalist purposes. Questioning them is my way of taking responsibility in the face of that angle,” explains the Montréal-Nord resident.
« Ici, c’est pas chez nous, même si on a: “This isn’t home for us, even though we grew up here”
La relation avec le Mois de l’histoire d: People’s relationship with Black History Month is strongly coloured by each person’s experience and reality.
«Ici, c’est pas chez nous, même si on es: “This isn’t home for us, even though we were born and raised here,” Sherlyne says. Her words seem to resonate with the others. “Always having to work harder than everyone else, it gets hard… We carry the blame for others. We’ve all been told: ‘You’re not allowed to make mistakes, you have to do more, because when they see you, even if you made the same mistake as the others, for you it’ll be worse,’” says Shana, a 29-year-old author and writer. Both women feel that the February celebrations allow them to take their place in society.
Arrivé il y a quelques mois à peine d’Ha: Having arrived from Haiti just a few months ago, Horiol Desile Destine approaches this commemoration differently. For him, Black History Month is synonymous with unease. “I understand that, when you’re Black, you’re at the back… They set aside a month just to say: ‘Oh, they’re here.’ They put them in the spotlight for a month, and then afterwards, there’s nothing. I’d feel much better if this month didn’t exist,” the newcomer admits. Horiol Desire Destine tells us he didn’t know a Black History Month existed. The commemoration is only official in Canada, the United States and England, which explains why most newcomers don’t know it exists. Guerdy, who is sitting next to Horiol Desile Destine, agrees. Also new to Quebec, he wonders: “Why just one month for Black people? There should be gatherings for Black people all year long, where their importance in Quebec society would be explained.”
La discussion se dirige alors vers l’exp: The discussion then turns to each person’s own experience of Black History Month. “I haven’t taken part in any events,” Gana confides. She explains that in Haiti, where she comes from, “Black History Month doesn’t exist.”
Les critiques suscitées par ces témoigna: The criticism raised by these accounts calls into question the primary mission of this commemoration. That bothers Youveline, an undergraduate student, in particular. “It’s Black History Month, not Black Month,” she corrects. “It’s still an important month for me, there’s a history behind it. There’s oppression in our history, and it’s something that continues to have an influence and still has repercussions on the community today,” she adds. She doesn’t hesitate to give an example: “It was during the month of February that my history teacher, on top of Quebec history, did a class on Martin Luther King,” she notes ironically, pointing to the absence of Black Canadian figures in the history that is taught.
Audrey, étudiante en multimédia âgée de: Audrey, a 20-year-old multimedia student, says Black History Month is a month like any other. “I’ve never celebrated Black history in any way,” she admits. “In February, it’s just my mom who talks to me about it. I don’t know much about it…” she adds. Unlike others, she experiences her Black identity differently. She admits that she only knows Haiti, her country of origin and her heritage, through her grandmother’s stories.
Jasmine, âgée de 16 ans, est élève à l’é: Jasmine, 16, a student at École secondaire Sophie-Barat, wants to highlight how invisible Black history is. “Other than in February, we don’t talk about it much,” she explains. She notes that even during the month devoted to Black history, the subject is barely addressed, if at all, in her classes. No activities are organized. “They put up a poster of Beyoncé and say they’re representing Black people,” she says mockingly.
« Je veux voir les petites madames de l’: “I want to see the little ladies from the grocery store”
« Il faut aller vers les familles ordina: “We need to reach out to ordinary families, who aren’t necessarily touched by this,” says Jean Alex. He is referring to activities organized during Black History Month that are often not accessible to a large part of the community. “There should be more activities in schools and in churches,” Gerdy suggests. “There are lots of people in evangelical churches. Come do activities with them,” Jean Alex adds. He explains that the community is found in these places and that it would be worthwhile to go there to offer activities and raise awareness about Black History Month. Jean Alex believes that many people aren’t included in Black History Month activities, and that these are the very people who could be interested if they were approached.
« J’ai l’impression qu’ils sont peut-êtr: “I get the feeling they might be forgotten,” says Shana. Many people are overlooked when these activities are promoted, and it’s always the same people who are asked to take part, Gana confides. She explains that, in her view, the organizers of these events are “running in place.” “I know what it’s about, but you invite me again, when there are people who need to know, who need to understand, and you never invite them,” she adds.
Pour Sherlyne, l’importance du Mois de l: For Sherlyne, the importance of Black History Month should be passed down “from generation to generation.” I think it’s by repeatedly confronting these young people with these specific realities that action will be taken,” she explains.
Au fil de la discussion, un thème revien: As the discussion goes on, one theme keeps coming up. The activities organized during Black History Month are exclusive. They don’t reach every part of the community and neglect those who are constantly left in the shadows, such as young people, seniors, newcomers or ordinary citizens who are far from the spotlight or from anti-racist circles, for example.
« Il devrait y avoir plus d’activités po: “There should be more activities for young people in the Black community: mentorship programs, programs where they’re introduced to Black authors and where they have spaces to express their passions, for example,” says Youveline. She notes that the events put on for the month are often aimed at older people. “Seventeen-year-olds aren’t necessarily going to go to an open-mic night at a bar,” she adds.
« Nous devrions rendre les possibilités: “We should make opportunities more accessible,” Youveline says again. “It’s often the same young people who get taken under someone’s wing and given a platform.” According to her, organizers often don’t want to do the work with young people who aren’t already engaged. They prefer to turn to young people who are knowledgeable about the issues and ready to talk about them and speak out.
« Il faudrait faire des activités pour i: “There should be activities to inform young people about the subject,” Jasmine chimes in. The 16-year-old student also explains that since the emergence of the Black Lives Matter movement, many young people have become aware of Black history. “Before, I had never heard of Black History Month,” she explains. She adds that at school, the cause came and went like a kind of trend. “They talked about it a bit when it was the main topic, but afterwards, it slowly faded away,” she explains.
Youveline souligne également que certain: Youveline also points out that some Black History Month events charge admission, which can make them less accessible for some people. “Charging for an event isn’t necessarily the best way to get people to come,” she explains. “For families, it’s not easy,” Jean Alex maintains.
Alors que la conversation tourne autour: As the conversation turns to solutions and ideas for initiatives, Audrey explains that the dialogue is giving her lots of ideas for events to organize for her community. The young woman, who is passionate about skateboarding, adds that “nobody thinks of Black people when it comes to skateboarding.” She thinks, for instance, that an event could be held at a skatepark for young people who don’t have access to events aimed at people over 25. “I’m thinking I could literally create an event to get more young people from Black communities into skateboarding, roller skating and biking,” she says.
Alors que la soirée tire à sa fin, le ma: As the evening draws to a close, the unease that was present in the room at the start seems to have faded, giving way to a warmer atmosphere. Despite the diversity of the participants’ experiences, a certain sense of cohesion sets in. Over a meal, the conversations bring together young people and newcomers, and the hope for a more inclusive February grows.
